title: Kernel orchestration casebook: fusion, paged paths, and FlashAttention interactions
content:
Purpose
This is a working casebook capturing experiments, heuristics, and hypotheses about orchestration-level decisions that influence which attention kernel (FlashAttention / paged / fused ops) is chosen at runtime and the performance fallout. Goal is to consolidate microbenchmarks, scheduler traces, and action items for follow-up optimizations and guardrails.

Context and motivation
- We already have multiple 'good' kernels: FlashAttention variants for contiguous KV, paged/flash-paged for long contexts, and fused-microkernels for small batches or model-specific layouts.
- In production we observe intermittent latency tails for x-large prompt shapes where the runtime flips between paged and fused code paths mid-stream. Suspect orchestration (scheduler, prefetch timing, and kernel-switch windows) is a major contributor.

High-level hypotheses (ranked)
1) Kernel switch hysteresis is too narrow: short-lived throughput variance triggers kernel selection thrashing, causing cache/alloc churn and extra kernel startup cost.
2) Prefetch ordering vs. kernel choice: a paged-prefetch path may have prefetched pages for a paged kernel; if scheduler later switches to fused/flash, those prefetched resources are wasted and increase contention.
3) Small-batch fusion fallbacks: fused ops have better latency for tiny sequence lengths but suffer when batch coalescing later increases sequence length — transition costs are high.
4) KV cache alignment and memory slab fragmentation amplify kernel startup jitter (allocation + scratchpad setup).

Experiment matrix (what we ran)
- Benchmark harness: local tracebench extended with orchestration toggles (switch-window, prefetch-delay-ms, hysteresis-ms). Replayed 10k real-request traces from prod-sample (anon).
- Shapes: short(64x32), medium(1024x2), long(8192x1), ramping-mix (mix of 8 shapes to emulate chat).
- Kernels toggled: flash-contiguous v2, flash-paged v1, fused-smallbatch v3 (with and without prealloc scratchpad), and a 'null' baseline (CPU fallback).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency end-to-end, kernel-startup-time, allocator-syscalls/sec, GPU occupancy, prefetch-hits, stall-bytes.

Representative runs and notes
1) Ramping-mix (default orchestration) -> p99 spikes at ~420ms; kernel logs show rapid alternation between flash-paged and fused-smallbatch across adjacent requests. Allocator syscalls spike at the same time.
  - Kernel-startup-time median increased from 0.8ms to 3.6ms during spike window.
  - Hypothesis: thrash due to narrow hysteresis + prefetch waste.

2) Increase hysteresis window to 40ms -> p99 reduced to 280ms, allocator syscalls down 60% during same workload. But p50 increased slightly (~5ms) for short requests.
  - Tradeoff: added latency for strictly short, but stabilizes tail.

3) Disable paged-prefetch (lazy-on-demand) -> p99 reduced to 260ms for long-shape-heavy runs; however throughput for long single-stream sequences decreased (observed extra per-page latency).
  - Indicates prefetch helps steady long streams but hurts mixed workloads by adding contention when kernel switches.

4) Force fused path for smallbatch-heavy traces with prealloc scratchpad -> reduces p50 by ~12% and p95 by ~10% with no increase in p99. Prealloc avoids allocator churn.

5) Stress test: artificially cause coalescing (combine small requests) -> fused kernel gets chosen initially but as sequence lengths increase the runtime switches to flash; when switching, the scratchpad deallocation + new kernel init adds ~5-12ms per switch, adding to tail.

Micro-observations (from tracing)
- Kernel selection decision points are invoked in two places: route-time (initial) and post-batching (scheduler). These two may disagree because batching changes effective shape.
- Prefetch kick-off is scheduled relative to the initial decision; if the scheduler later changes kernel, prefetch remains in-flight. No cancel mechanism exists today.
- Scratchpad allocations use a best-effort slab allocator; fragmentation grows when mixing paged allocations and fused scratchpads of different sizes.

Immediate mitigations tried (and artifact links)
- Hysteresis tuning: raising threshold to 20-50ms reduces switching. (see PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/812)
- Prefetch cancellation: prototype cancels in-flight prefetch when kernel changes; reduced wasted prefetches by ~78% in lab; needs safety checks.
- Prealloc scratchpad for fused kernels when expected coalescing probability > 0.6 (simple heuristic based on traffic class).

Longer-term proposals
1) Two-phase kernel decision: initial decision at route-time plus a validation step post-batching that only allows switches if projected cost delta > estimated switch cost + contention penalty. Requires switch-cost model.
2) Prefetch as idempotent/cancellable tasks with backpressure signals to scheduler. If a prefetch cannot be completed before switch-window, cancel to avoid memory contention.
3) Per-tenant kernel policy profiles: e.g., customer A (chatty short messages) biases fused-smallbatch; customer B (long docs) biases paged-prefetch. Persist suggestion scores and warm start selection.
4) Improve scratchpad allocator: segregate pools for paged vs fused kernels; add compacting passes on low-traffic windows.
5) Warm-up vs steady-state selection: for continued sequences, allow more aggressive prefetch and pin kernel choice for the session.

Open questions and next actions
- Need an accurate model of kernel switch cost (empirical vs analytical). Action: microbench a deterministic switch cost matrix across shapes and GPU families. (owner: Ravi)
- How often do real production sessions benefit from prefetch cancellation vs always-on prefetch? Action: run A/B across steady-state long sessions. (owner: Elena)
- Implement prefetch cancellation prototype in canary and monitor allocator syscalls and GPU mem usage. (owner: Samir)
- Consider exposing a per-route policy flag 'pin_kernel_for_session' for enterprise customers that want deterministic latency.

Runbook snippets / commands used
- tracebench replay: ./tracebench --trace-file traces/prod-sample-2025-10-21.tr --orchestration-hysteresis-ms 40 --enable-prefetch-cancel=true --out results/exp-hyst-40.log
- micro switch matrix: python tools/switch_matrix.py --gpu a100 --shapes 64x32,1024x2,8192x1 --repeat 2000 --out switch-matrix-a100.csv

Notes to self / rough ideas
- Could we learn a cheap decision function (lightweight NN) to predict effective kernel choice after batching finishes? Might be faster than heuristics and could encode tenant patterns.
- Add tracing fields: chosen_kernel, prefetch_started_at, prefetch_cancelled_at, scratchpad_pool_id to make postmortem simpler.

Appendix: key trace excerpts
- TraceID: 6f9b2a (ramping-mix run): sequence of decisions: flash-paged -> fused-smallbatch -> flash-paged -> fused-smallbatch within 120ms. Allocation spike coincident.
- Switch cost sample (A100): flash-paged -> fused-smallbatch median 3.2ms, reverse 2.9ms.

Summary
This casebook consolidates evidence that orchestration-level choices (hysteresis, prefetch timing, scratchpad allocation) are first-order contributors to tail latency when multiple attention kernels are available. Short-term wins exist (hysteresis tuning, prealloc pools, prefetch cancellation). Longer-term work should reduce decision flip-flopping and make kernel switches either cheaper or rarer via better modeling and per-session pinning.

Action items (short list)
- [ ] Microbench switch-cost matrix (Ravi)
- [ ] Run A/B for prefetch-cancel in canary fleet (Elena)
- [ ] Implement prealloc scratchpad heuristic for fused kernels (Samir)
- [ ] Instrument extra tracing fields in one-week sprint (Aisha)

End of draft.
